title: IELTS Academic Reading Practice Test 20
instructions: You should spend about 20 minutes on each passage. Answer all questions.

passages.title: Water Uphill
passages.text:
A. Before engines, moving anything heavy over land was the expensive part of any journey. A horse that could pull a cart carrying a modest load along a rutted road could pull a barge carrying many times that weight along a still waterway, and the difference was not marginal but decisive. Where a river ran the right way, bulk goods moved cheaply; where it did not, they largely did not move at all.

B. The engineering problem was never digging the channel but crossing high ground. A canal must be level or nearly so, and the device that made hilly country navigable — a chamber with gates at each end that raises or lowers a vessel by filling or emptying — is old, simple in principle and unforgiving in practice. Each operation consumes a lockful of water from the upper level, and a busy flight of locks can drain a summit faster than any stream refills it.

C. Water supply, not construction, therefore determined which routes succeeded. Summit levels needed reservoirs, feeder channels and sometimes pumping engines simply to stay usable in dry months, and several ambitious routes were completed and then found to be unreliable for exactly this reason. The most profitable canals were frequently not the most impressive ones but those crossing terrain that happened to supply them.

D. What the canals carried mattered more than what they cost. Coal, stone, lime, timber and grain are heavy, low in value per tonne and tolerant of slow travel, which is precisely the profile that water transport suits and road transport does not. Industries that had been tied to their fuel source could now be sited elsewhere, and the geography of manufacturing reorganised itself around the new network within a generation.

E. Decline was rapid and is usually attributed to the railway alone, which is only part of the account. Canals were fragmented among many small companies with incompatible dimensions, so a barge that fitted one waterway could not always pass along the next; the railway offered a single operator, a single gauge over long distances and speed that mattered increasingly as goods became more valuable per tonne. Fragmentation lost the traffic as much as competition did.

F. The reuse of the surviving network has been almost entirely unplanned. Channels dug for coal now carry recreational craft; towpaths built for horses serve walkers and cyclists; the corridors themselves have become continuous habitat through built-up areas where little else is continuous. None of this was foreseen by anyone who financed the original works, and the value now derived is of a kind the original accounts had no way to record.

passages.title: A Skill the Brain Was Not Built For
passages.text:
Speech is old enough that the human brain has specialised machinery for it: children in ordinary circumstances acquire a spoken language without instruction, on a predictable schedule, and cannot easily be prevented from doing so. Reading is different in kind. Writing is a few thousand years old, far too recent for any dedicated apparatus to have evolved, and reading is therefore assembled out of systems that developed for other purposes — visual recognition, spoken language, attention — connected together by explicit teaching.

The consequence is that reading must be taught and speech need not, a distinction with more practical weight than it is usually given. A child who is spoken to will learn to speak. A child who is surrounded by books will not necessarily learn to read, and the failure is not a failure of exposure or of motivation but of instruction in something genuinely arbitrary: which marks correspond to which sounds.

The evidence on how that instruction should proceed is unusually settled for education research, and unusually badly transmitted into practice. Systematic teaching of letter–sound relationships produces better outcomes than approaches that rely on inferring words from context and pictures, and the advantage is largest for the children who struggle most — those from homes with less spoken language, and those with underlying difficulties. Approaches that appeared to work in classrooms often did so because the strongest readers were compensating.

Guessing from context is what poor readers do, not what good ones do, which inverts an assumption that shaped teaching for decades. A skilled reader identifies words rapidly and largely automatically, and uses context to resolve meaning rather than identity. Teaching a beginner to predict a word from the picture beside it trains the strategy of the struggling reader and gives the appearance of progress while the underlying skill is not being built.

What follows decoding is where the harder problem lies. Once words can be recognised, comprehension is limited by vocabulary and by knowledge of the subject, and neither is acquired as a general skill — both are built word by word and topic by topic. A reader who decodes fluently but knows nothing about the topic understands little, which is why comprehension scores track background knowledge closely and why time removed from history, science and geography in order to practise comprehension has tended to lower it.

The gap between what is established and what is done remains the field's central embarrassment. Teaching methods persist for reasons of training, materials, institutional habit and the reasonable observation by teachers that most of their pupils learn regardless. The children for whom the method matters are precisely those least likely to be noticed as evidence, since their difficulties are readily attributed to circumstances outside the classroom.

passages.title: Who Pays for the Paper
passages.text:
Academic publishing has an economic structure that would be considered indefensible in almost any other industry, and it persists because the people whose behaviour would have to change are not the people paying. Researchers, funded largely by public money, produce papers and give them to publishers without payment. Other researchers review them without payment. Editors are frequently unpaid or nominally paid. The publisher then sells access back to the institutions that employed everyone involved.

The margins this produces are the ones usually quoted, and they are striking, but the more interesting question is why the arrangement is stable. The answer is that the product being bought is not the paper, which is often available elsewhere, but the journal's reputation — and reputation is exactly what cannot be competed away by a new entrant offering the same service more cheaply. A researcher's career depends on where the work appears, so the incentive to publish in an established venue survives any argument about cost.

Open access was intended to break this and has partly done so, at the cost of moving the problem. When the reader stops paying, the author must, and article processing charges at prestigious journals now run to sums that exclude researchers without substantial grants. A system that was inaccessible to readers in poorer institutions has become, in part, inaccessible to authors in them, which is a different distribution of the same exclusion rather than its removal.

The charging model also created an incentive that the subscription model did not. A publisher paid per article accepted has a reason to accept more articles, and the appearance of journals that publish almost anything for a fee follows directly. The response — lists of approved venues, indexing criteria, institutional rules — has produced a compliance apparatus that consumes researcher time and does not clearly outperform the judgement it replaced.

Peer review, the process the whole structure is organised around, has weaker evidence behind it than its centrality suggests. It is slow, inconsistent between reviewers on the same paper, and demonstrably poor at detecting error or fabrication, which it was never designed to detect. It remains valuable as a filter and as a source of improvement to papers, and the reasonable position is that it does something useful less well than is generally assumed rather than that it does nothing.

What has changed the situation most is not reform but circumvention. Researchers now routinely post work before or without formal publication, and in several fields the version everyone reads is the freely posted one while the journal version exists mainly for the record. The formal system has not been replaced and has quietly ceased to be the route by which most people actually encounter the work.
